paras: The Libby whitecap attacks were assaults in early 1903 by a masked band, called "Kuklux" or "whitecaps" in the press, on a colony of Black landowners near Libby in eastern Nacogdoches County, Texas. On the night of January 28, the band fired into the home of a Black man, named Jim Pleasant, Jim Morris or Jim Martin, and carried him off; he was not found and was supposed murdered. Dispatches said the colony was "terror stricken" and leaving, and Black papers called it a "reign of terror."

According to the Wichita Searchlight, the colony had lived there for years and had bought its homes and built churches and schoolhouses. The Daily Ardmoreite reported that eight "well to do negroes" had been forced from their homes since Christmas, and the Houston Post said trouble had been brewing between some Black residents and "a few of the whites." A Nacogdoches letter in the Indianapolis Freeman, written before the attack, said three preachers had been whipped and 12 or 15 other men beaten there in a year.

Shortly before the main attack, the band went to the home of Jess (or Jesse) Robertson; accounts of his fate differ. On Wednesday night, January 28, masked men shot the door of Pleasant's house "full of holes" and fired into it with six-shooters and shotguns. In the Searchlight's account, his wife escaped with their baby, but he was captured and carried into the woods. His clothes were found in the woods, and after the band returned and burned his barn, it was supposed his body had been burned.

The sheriff took a posse to the scene, and Constable Doc Watson and Deputy Hiram Morris went to Libby. The Searchlight said they, a Deputy Slay and several citizens searched two days and nights without a trace of Pleasant. On February 3, a dispatch reported eight Black residents of the Libby community whipped and forced to leave. A note signed "WHITECAPPERS" then ordered Jim Anderson, a Black man near Libby, to leave within four days or be killed.

Officers at first thought the attack on Pleasant would "terminate the trouble." Later they said they knew the ringleader, who was hiding in the pine woods, and alleged he had "put Jim Pleasant away" to obtain Pleasant's wife. A Houston item in the Cleveland Gazette said the terror spread to a settlement ten miles from Nacogdoches, where ten were beaten, Anderson was shot dead, a dozen homes were burned, and residents fled to Oklahoma. No report of an arrest, inquest or trial was found.

White papers ran brief Nacogdoches dispatches: the Houston Post's "Negro Taken from His Home," the Bryan Morning Eagle's "Kuklux at Work" and the Daily Ardmoreite's "Terrorizing the Negros." They gave no comment on the attackers, and the story shrank as it traveled, to one sentence in Bryan and one line in a Mississippi weekly.

The Black press used sharper language. The Searchlight headlined its fuller dispatch "Kill Blacks and Destroy their Homes" and alone reported the note to Anderson and the officers' allegation. The Cleveland Gazette wrote of "our people" and "whitecap outrages" and stressed the flight from the county.

The man carried off is Jim Pleasant in the Post and the Searchlight, Jim Morris in the Bryan paper and Jim Martin in the Ardmoreite; all describe one attack. The Bryan paper said Robertson's "horse" was whipped to death, the Ardmoreite that he was "horse whipped to death," and the Searchlight that he was beaten insensible, swore out warrants and disappeared. The Searchlight has Anderson only threatened, while the Gazette says he was shot dead.

reader.title: Libby whitecap attacks
bases: A masked band the papers called 'Kuklux' or 'whitecaps' attacked, whipped, warned and drove out Black landowners of a settled colony near Libby, carried off one man and burned property, over several weeks (A3, A6, A7, A9).

The Houston Post's Jan. 30 dispatch (A3), a separate Nacogdoches dispatch carried in Bryan and Ardmore (A5, A6) and a Feb. 7 dispatch in the Wichita Searchlight (A9) agree that masked men fired into a Black man's house near Libby on Jan. 28 and carried him off, though they differ on his name.

accounts.label: Houston Post Nacogdoches dispatch (from telephone report to sheriff)
accounts.gist: Masked men shot up Jim Pleasant's house on the 28th and carried him off; he is supposed killed and the colony is leaving in droves; trouble had been brewing between some Black residents and a few whites, and officers expected the attack to end it.

accounts.label: Nacogdoches wire dispatch (Bryan, Ardmore)
accounts.gist: An organized Kuklux band has forced Black residents out since Christmas, whipped Robertson (or his horse) to death and carried off a Black schoolteacher, Morris or Martin, supposed murdered and burned in his barn.

accounts.label: Feb. 7 Nacogdoches dispatch in the Black press
accounts.gist: Whitecaps captured Pleasant as his wife and baby fled, burned his barn, beat Robertson, who later vanished, and threatened Anderson in writing; officers know the ringleader and allege Pleasant was put away to obtain his wife.

accounts.label: Houston item in the Cleveland Gazette
accounts.gist: The reign of terror continued at a settlement ten miles from Nacogdoches, with ten beaten, Jim Anderson shot dead, many missing, a dozen homes burned and residents fleeing to Oklahoma.

framing.detail: Short Nacogdoches dispatches under 'Negro Taken from His Home', 'Kuklux at Work' and 'Terrorizing the Negros' report the attacks without comment on the attackers.
Follow-ups shrink to one sentence: eight 'nogroes' whipped and forced to leave; Black residents 'panic-stricken' over a mob.
The Searchlight headlines 'Kill Blacks and Destroy their Homes' and 'Reign of Terror', stresses the colony's owned homes, churches and schools, and describes Anderson as never in trouble.
The Cleveland Gazette speaks of 'our people' and 'whitecap outrages' and reports flight to Oklahoma.
